description: Our team combines the expertise of a Web Developer, AI Specialist, Dedicated Researcher, Clinical psychologist, Multimedia Graphic Designer, and a 3D & Motion Designer. We believe that safeguarding astronauts during deep-space missions requires a holistic approach—one that monitors both physical vital signs and psychological well-being in extreme environments.
summary:
HALO is a web-based wellbeing companion for astronauts on long missions. It combines wearable data sleep, heart rate, activity with a daily check in under two minutes covering mood, stress, loneliness, depression-scale and crew questions. Over about 14 days it learns each astronaut's personal normal, then shows a green, yellow or red status with the reasons behind it. When a trend worsens, it offers support such as breathing exercises; in an emergency it alerts base and the crew doctor. A private memory collection keeps photos and messages from loved ones close. HALO works offline, keeps data on the device, never diagnoses and never suggests medication.

This addresses the challenge directly: on a Mars mission, messages take 20–22 minutes one way, so astronauts must notice health changes themselves before Earth can help. NASA lists behavioral health monitoring as an open research gap, and existing tools each cover only one piece Astroskin the body, CIMON emotion from speech, ESA's VR relaxation sessions. None joins body, mind and crew into one daily picture.

It matters because health is connected: when physical, psychological or social health falls, the others follow. HALO monitors them together, compares each person only with themselves, and gives support without waiting for Earth.
details: Background and evidence NASA's behavioral risk page says isolation and confinement can raise the risk of anxiety and depression and can affect sleep, morale and decision making. It lists journaling, windows and privacy as countermeasures but gives no efficacy data. Crews respond very differently: in the Mars-520 simulation, three of six crew accumulated stress and three did not, so one threshold for everyone misses people. Astronauts sleep about 6 hours in space (seven studies) against 7.9 hours on Earth in a Shuttle crew survey, and about three-quarters of Shuttle and ISS astronauts used sleep medication, which sped falling asleep but did not lengthen sleep (NASA sleep Evidence Report). Basner et al. (2013) tracked a crew of six with wrist sensors for 520 days: sedentariness rose, sleep time increased by 8.4% and light exposure fell. Existing tools each cover one dimension. Astroskin (Hexoskin with NASA and the Canadian Space Agency) measures activity, heart, breathing, skin temperature, blood pressure and blood oxygen, but covers the body only. CIMON uses IBM Watson Tone Analyzer to detect emotion from the tone of conversation and mainly assists with tasks. ESA's VR headset experiment (HTC Vive Focus 3, EveryWear app) pairs VR video with questionnaires for isolation and stress. Our sources do not describe daily tracking or early warnings for the last two. The gap is integration, a personal baseline and early warning. How we built HALO 1. Problem analysis: We analyzed the problem and its impact using NASA sources, covering sleep quality, isolation and behavior. 2. Research and gap analysis: We read NASA documents and analog studies to choose indicators, and found that existing tools (CIMON, Astroskin, ESA VR Mental Care) each solve only part of the problem. 3. Questions and data: From our sources, we chose the daily check-in questions and the data HALO needs. 4. Indicators: Sleep duration and quality, heart rate, activity, mood, stress, loneliness and fatigue. Daily depression-scale questions, and crew questions on team missions. 5. Personal baseline: Learn each astronaut's normal over about 14 days, then compare every signal only with that person's own normal. 6. Status logic: One bad day does nothing. Yellow means a trend has formed across days in at least two signals. Red means a sustained change in several signals. Self-report counts for no more than the passive signals. *[confirm weights]* 7. Support logic: Breathing exercises, contact with a crewmate, routine adjustments and the memory collection. Red always offers "talk to a professional or the crew doctor". 8. Visual identity: We chose the color palette and created the HALO visual identity. 9. Prototype: We used AI to help make a first design of the website in Figma, then built the 3D astronaut avatar. 10. Working website: We turned the Figma prototype into a working website with the check-in, scoring and offline storage. 11. Technical details: Html css java script What HALO does and how it works • What HALO does with it: HALO turns scattered signals into one personal picture. It syncs wearable data (design: Bluetooth link to a device such as Astroskin), scores the daily check-in, compares every signal with the person's own baseline, and computes the green/yellow/red status with the reasons behind it. ]* • What comes out: A daily status with reasons, early support actions, emergency alerts to base and the crew doctor, and personal settings such as medication reminders for chronic conditions. They see there health on the screen The daily check-in Stress: 0-4 (PSS-4) -How often today have you felt that you were unable to control the important things in your life? -How often today have you felt confident about your ability to handle your personal problems? -How often today have you felt that things were going your way? -How often today have you felt difficulties were piling up so high that you could not overcome them? Depression:0-4 (PHQ-9) -Little interest or pleasure in doing things. -Feeling down, depressed, or hopeless. -Trouble falling or staying asleep, or sleeping too much. -Feeling tired or having little energy. -Poor appetite or overeating. -Feeling bad about yourself or that you are a failure or have let yourself or family down. -Thoughts that you would be better off dead or of hurting yourself in some way. How lonely do you feel today? 0-10 How is your mood today? 0-10 Implementation steps in the build 1. Sync wearable data (design: Bluetooth link to a device such as Astroskin). 2. Build the daily check-in and score. 3. Add the green/yellow/red status with reasons. 4. Add support actions, the memory collection and emergency alerts. 5. Add personal settings, such as medication reminders for chronic conditions. 6. Test with simulated data. Testing We tested with simulated crew data modelled on the Mars-520 pattern, where half the crew drift and half stay stable. All simulated data is labelled as simulated. Tools, coding languages, hardware and software • Design: Figma, Canva, Adobe Illustrator • 3D: Blender, used for the 3D astronaut avatar • Website: Visual Studio Code; built with help from Copilot, an AI tool. https://sketchfab.com/feed • AI tools: see section 5. Benefits and goals HALO's goal is to protect astronauts' mental and physical health when help from Earth is far away. It aims to give early support before a small change becomes a serious problem. Its method monitors physical and psychological signals together, works offline, and does not depend on Earth. Against alternatives: Astroskin tracks the body only, CIMON works in conversation, and ESA's VR experiment gives sessions; HALO joins all of this and adds a daily, personal baseline with early warning. Working features, limits and future plans • Working features: it measures and blends all the body and mind indecators • Limits and unfinished parts: The wearable link is a design, not a working integration. The status weights are not confirmed. All testing used simulated data. Only the prototype is done • Future plans: make it easier to access and add a calling feature 3. NASA data and resources At least one NASA resource is required to qualify for a Global Award, so fill all links. Resource 1: NASA CBS Problem Statement and behavioral risk material • What we used from it: The problem statement on isolation, confinement and communication delay, and the open research gap on validated behavioral health monitoring (BMed2). • How it helped our solution: It defined the problem and told us validated monitoring measures are an open gap, which HALO targets. Resource 2: NASA sleep Evidence Report • What we used from it: In-space sleep duration (about 6 hours, seven studies), the 7.9 hours Earth baseline, and the finding that about three-quarters of Shuttle and ISS astronauts used sleep medication without lengthening sleep. • How it helped our solution: It justified making sleep a core passive indicator and comparing each astronaut only with their own baseline. https://www.nasa.gov/reference/risk-of-behavioral-changes-and-psychiatric-disorders/ https://www.nasa.gov/reference/risk-of-inadequate-teamwork/ https://www.nasa.gov/hrp/hazards/ 4. Other resources and source credits Resource 1: Basner et al. (2013), Mars-520 mission study • Link: *[ ]* • What we used from it: The 520-day wrist-sensor findings (sedentariness rose, sleep time increased 8.4%, light exposure fell) and the finding that three of six crew accumulated stress while three did not. • How it helped our solution: It showed one threshold misses people, grounding the personal baseline and two-signal trend logic, and it is the pattern for our simulated test data. Resource 2: Astroskin (Hexoskin with NASA and the Canadian Space Agency) • What we used from it: Its measured signals, as the model for the wearable data HALO syncs. • How it helped our solution: It defined the physical layer of the input. Resource 3: CIMON and ESA's VR headset experiment (HTC Vive Focus 3, EveryWear app) • What we used from it: Their capabilities, as the psychological layer we integrate. • How it helped our solution: It showed existing tools cover one dimension each, defining the gap. 5. AI and SI use We used AI tools to support our work. AI did not create our idea for solving the challenge. The idea, the research and the visual identity were made by our team. • Website development: We used Git hub copilt to help us build the website. • First website design: We used figma to help create a first design of the website, based on the color palette we chose. • Visual identity: Our team created the HALO visual identity from our research. We used illustrator only to help improve it and show it clearly in Figma. • Simulated test data: the codes were in ai 6. Team and workflow Team and roles • Lina Ahmed Elsayed, Leader and Visual Designer: Coordinated tasks, researched sources, designed the UX and HALO's visual identity. • Zainab Abdulwahab, Co-Leader and Clinical Psychology Researcher: Coordinated tasks, researched sources, and developed the daily health questions and required data. • Omar Emad Hegazy, AI and Software Developer: Organized AI prompts around our research and turned it into the website design. • Andrew Emad, Designer and 3D Artist: Organized research data visually and created the 3D models for the presentation. Collaboration and milestones We met on site when needed to assign tasks, held Discord meetings while working to help each other and see what was missing, and used WhatsApp to share sources and tasks. Day 1 (Nov 12): research across all sources (7 hours), then 1 hour to compile the website ideas. Day 2 (Nov 13): built the prototype, the 3D avatar and the presentation.
